title: Fixed window counter
prompt: Arrange `allow(now)` for a fixed window rate limiter: at most `limit` requests per `windowMs`, with the counter reset whenever a new window starts. The clock is injected as `now`.
explanation: The window index is `now / windowMs`, so every request in the same second shares one counter, and the counter resets to zero when a request lands in a new window. The check is `count >= limit` before incrementing, so exactly `limit` requests pass. It is the cheapest limiter (one integer per key) and maps neatly onto a MongoDB or Redis document keyed by `user:window` with an atomic `$inc`. Its weakness shows at the boundary: 3 requests at t=999 and 3 more at t=1000 means 6 requests in 2 ms, double the intended rate. Sliding windows and token buckets fix that.

title: Leaky bucket meter
prompt: Fill the gaps in a leaky bucket: each request adds one unit of water, the bucket drains at a constant rate, and a request that would overflow the capacity is rejected.
explanation: The bucket level drains linearly with elapsed time but can never go below empty, hence `Math.max(0, ...)`. A request is accepted only if adding one unit keeps the level within `capacity`. A token bucket allows a burst up to its capacity and then a steady rate. A leaky bucket used as a queue instead smooths output to a constant rate, which suits a downstream that cannot absorb bursts, such as a MongoDB primary under write load. The clock is a parameter, so tests are deterministic.

title: Capped exponential backoff
prompt: Arrange the retry loop: call `op`, and on failure sleep `base * 2^attempt` milliseconds capped at `capMs`, giving up after `maxAttempts`. Sleeping goes through a fake clock.
expectedOutput:
attempt 0 failed, sleeping 100ms
attempt 1 failed, sleeping 200ms
attempt 2 failed, sleeping 400ms
attempt 3 failed, sleeping 500ms
ok at t=1200ms
explanation: Each failed attempt doubles the wait (100, 200, 400, ...), so a struggling dependency gets more and more time to recover, and the cap stops the delay from growing without limit (the fourth wait is 500 rather than 800). The `attempt + 1 >= maxAttempts` check rethrows on the last attempt instead of sleeping for nothing. Injecting the clock makes the schedule testable without real sleeps. In production you would add jitter so that many clients do not retry at the same moments. MongoDB drivers make a single immediate retry for retryable reads and writes and leave longer backoff to the application.

title: Token bucket vs fixed window vs leaky
prompt: Compare the three classic rate-limiting algorithms.
question: Explain how a token bucket, a leaky bucket and a fixed window counter each work, how they treat bursts, and when you would choose each.
keyPoints: Token bucket: tokens refill at rate r up to capacity b; each request spends a token; allows bursts up to b, then a sustained rate r
Leaky bucket: requests fill a bucket that drains at a constant rate; smooths output; excess overflows and is dropped or queued
Fixed window: a counter per time window, reset at boundaries; cheap, but allows up to 2x the limit across a window boundary
State cost: fixed window is one counter; token bucket is tokens plus a last-refill timestamp; both O(1) per key
Choice: token bucket for APIs that tolerate bursts, leaky bucket to protect a downstream that needs steady load, fixed window for simple cheap quotas
Refill is computed lazily from elapsed time on each request rather than by a background timer
modelAnswer: A token bucket holds up to b tokens and refills at r tokens per second, computed lazily from the elapsed time on each request. A request proceeds if a token is available, so clients can burst up to b and then sustain r. A leaky bucket treats requests as water draining at a fixed rate. It enforces a smooth output rate and drops or queues anything that would overflow, so it is good for protecting a downstream, such as a database primary, that cannot absorb spikes. A fixed window counter increments a counter keyed by the current window (say, the current minute) and rejects requests once it hits the limit. It is the cheapest option, but a client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next, getting double the rate. All three need O(1) state per key. I would use a token bucket for public API quotas where bursts are fine, a leaky bucket or queue in front of fragile backends, and a fixed window for coarse quotas where boundary bursts do not matter.
hint: Think about what each one does with 100 requests arriving in the same millisecond.
explanation: The token bucket separates burst size (capacity) from sustained rate (refill rate), which is why it is the default for API gateways. The leaky bucket gives a constant output rate. Fixed windows have the boundary problem, which sliding window logs and counters fix. Interviewers often follow up by asking how to make any of these work across many app servers sharing one store, for example a MongoDB document updated with an atomic `$inc` or `findOneAndUpdate`.

title: Only retry what is safe
prompt: Fill the gaps so a client retries only requests that are both idempotent and failed with a transient error.
expectedOutput:
GET 503 -> retry
PUT 429 -> retry
POST 503 -> fail fast
GET 400 -> fail fast
PUT 404 -> fail fast
explanation: A retry is only safe when repeating the operation cannot change the outcome (idempotent: GET, PUT, DELETE), and only useful when the failure is transient (503 overloaded, 429 throttled, timeouts). Retrying a 400 just repeats a bug, and retrying a POST may charge a card twice. Both conditions must hold, hence `&&`. MongoDB solves the non-idempotent case for single-document writes: with retryable writes the driver attaches the session id (`lsid`) and a `txnNumber`, so the server recognises a retried insert and returns the original result instead of applying it again. To make an HTTP POST safe you need the same idea, an idempotency key.

title: Token bucket with lazy refill
prompt: Arrange `tryAcquire(now)`: refill tokens from the elapsed time (capped at capacity), then spend one token if one is available.
explanation: No background timer is needed: on each call the bucket credits `elapsed * rate` tokens, capped at capacity so an idle client cannot save up an unlimited burst. Updating `last` on every call, including denials, keeps the credit accurate. The first three calls drain the initial burst, the fourth is denied, and after a long idle period the bucket refills only to 3. Storing just `tokens` and `last` per key makes this easy to keep in a shared store. The read-modify-write then needs to be atomic, for example a compare-and-set on a version, or a single `findOneAndUpdate` with an update pipeline in MongoDB.

title: Why retryable writes are safe
prompt: Explain MongoDB retryable writes and retryable reads.
question: A network error hits right after the driver sends an insert to the primary, so the client does not know whether it was applied. Explain how MongoDB retryable writes make the automatic retry safe, what their limits are, and how retryable reads differ.
keyPoints: The driver attaches a logical session id (lsid) and an increasing txnNumber to each retryable write
The server records the outcome per (lsid, txnNumber) in config.transactions, replicated through the oplog, so a retry with the same pair returns the stored result instead of re-executing
The driver retries once, on retryable errors (network errors, NotWritablePrimary, errors labelled RetryableWriteError), after selecting a server again, which covers a primary failover
Only some operations qualify: single-document writes, insertMany, bulkWrite without multi-document updates or deletes, findAndModify; updateMany and deleteMany are not retryable
retryWrites=true is the default in modern drivers; retryable reads retry once on network or not-primary errors, which is safe because reads have no side effects
Application-level retries beyond the single retry still need idempotency, or transactions retried by error label
modelAnswer: With retryable writes the driver runs each write in a logical session and tags it with the session id (lsid) and a txnNumber that increases with each write. The server keeps the outcome of the latest txnNumber per session in config.transactions, which is replicated through the oplog. If the driver resends the same (lsid, txnNumber) after a network error, or after a failover to a new primary, the server sees that it has already executed the write and returns the recorded result instead of inserting twice. The driver retries exactly once, after server selection finds a writable primary, and only for retryable errors such as network errors, NotWritablePrimary or anything with the RetryableWriteError label. Only operations with a well-defined single result qualify: single-document inserts, updates and deletes, findAndModify, and bulk inserts. Multi-document updateMany and deleteMany are not retryable. Retryable reads are simpler: reads have no side effects, so the driver just retries once on a transient error. Anything beyond that one retry, such as during a long outage, is up to the application and needs its own idempotency or a transaction retried on TransientTransactionError.
hint: What two values let the server recognise that it has seen this exact write before?
explanation: Retryable writes give an exactly-once effect on top of at-least-once delivery: the driver may send the write twice, but the (lsid, txnNumber) dedup record turns the second send into a no-op that returns the first result. This is the same pattern as an idempotency key table, built into the database and replicated so it survives elections. Knowing which operations are excluded (multi-document updates and deletes) is a common SDE3 follow-up.

title: Full jitter vs equal jitter
prompt: Fill the gaps to compute AWS-style full jitter (uniform in [0, ceiling)) and equal jitter (half fixed, half random) with a seeded Random.
expectedOutput:
attempt 0: full=72 equal=86
attempt 1: full=136 equal=168
attempt 2: full=123 equal=261
attempt 3: full=221 equal=510
attempt 4: full=1064 equal=1332
attempt 5: full=1806 equal=1903
explanation: Without jitter, every client that failed at the same moment also retries at the same moments, so retries arrive in synchronised waves (the thundering herd). Full jitter picks uniformly between 0 and the exponential ceiling, which spreads load best and usually finishes the work fastest. Equal jitter keeps at least half the backoff, guaranteeing a minimum wait while still desynchronising clients. `nextGaussian` would give negative and clustered values, which is the wrong distribution. Seeding the Random makes the schedule reproducible in tests.

title: Circuit breaker state machine
prompt: Arrange the breaker: OPEN rejects requests until the cool-down elapses, then lets a trial through in HALF_OPEN. A success closes it; a failed trial or `threshold` consecutive failures open it.
expectedOutput:
t=0 fail -> CLOSED
t=10 fail -> CLOSED
t=20 fail -> OPEN
t=500 rejected fast (OPEN)
t=1100 fail -> OPEN
t=1500 rejected fast (OPEN)
t=2200 ok -> CLOSED
t=2300 ok -> CLOSED
explanation: CLOSED passes traffic and counts failures. After `threshold` failures it trips to OPEN and fails fast, so callers stop wasting threads and timeouts on a dead dependency and the dependency gets time to recover. After the cool-down, the next request moves it to HALF_OPEN as a probe: success closes the circuit, and failure reopens it immediately without waiting for three more failures. Without the HALF_OPEN check, a bad probe would count as only one failure. Breakers complement the MongoDB driver, which already monitors servers and fails server selection after `serverSelectionTimeoutMS`; a breaker in the app stops request threads piling up while they wait for that timeout.

title: Semaphore bulkhead
prompt: Fill the gaps so at most two calls run against the dependency at once, and a third caller waits briefly and is then rejected instead of queueing forever.
expectedOutput:
a: admitted
b: admitted
c: rejected, bulkhead full
d: admitted
free permits: 0
explanation: A bulkhead gives each dependency its own bounded pool of concurrency, so a slow dependency can use up only its own permits rather than every request thread in the service. `tryAcquire` with a short timeout turns overload into a fast, explicit rejection, whereas plain `acquire` would queue without limit. Permits must be released when the call finishes. The MongoDB driver connection pool is the same idea: `maxPoolSize` caps concurrent connections per server, and `waitQueueTimeoutMS` (in newer drivers, `timeoutMS`) limits how long a thread waits for a connection before erroring.

title: Idempotency key dedup table
prompt: Arrange `charge`: if the idempotency key has been seen before, return the stored result; otherwise apply the charge, record the result under the key and return it.
lines: static String charge(String idempotencyKey, int amount) {
expectedOutput:
charged 30, balance 70
charged 30, balance 70 (replayed)
charged 10, balance 60
final balance 60
explanation: The client generates one key per logical operation and reuses it on every retry, so the server can turn at-least-once delivery into an exactly-once effect. Storing the full response rather than just "done" lets the retry receive the same answer as the original. In production the key insert and the side effect must be atomic. For example, insert into a MongoDB collection with a unique index on the key inside the same transaction as the balance update, so a crash cannot leave the charge applied without the key. MongoDB retryable writes do exactly this internally with `(lsid, txnNumber)` in `config.transactions`.

title: At-least-once vs exactly-once
prompt: Discuss delivery guarantees and how to get exactly-once effects.
question: Explain the difference between at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery. Why is exactly-once delivery impossible over an unreliable network, and how do real systems, including MongoDB, achieve exactly-once effects?
keyPoints: At-most-once: send once and never retry; messages may be lost
At-least-once: retry until acknowledged; messages may be duplicated, because a lost ack looks the same as a lost request
Exactly-once delivery is impossible end to end, because the sender cannot know whether the receiver processed a request whose ack was lost
Exactly-once effect = at-least-once delivery + idempotent or deduplicated processing on the receiver
Techniques: idempotency keys in a dedup table (unique index), naturally idempotent operations (set instead of increment), storing processed offsets atomically with results
MongoDB: retryable writes dedup by lsid + txnNumber; transactions retry the commit on UnknownTransactionCommitResult; change stream consumers resume from resume tokens
modelAnswer: At-most-once sends a message once and never retries, so failures lose data. At-least-once retries until it sees an acknowledgement, so it never loses data but can duplicate it. True exactly-once delivery is impossible over an unreliable network: if the acknowledgement is lost, the sender cannot tell whether the request was processed, so it must either risk a loss or risk a duplicate. What systems actually offer is an exactly-once effect: deliver at least once and make processing idempotent. You do that with idempotency keys recorded in a dedup table with a unique index and written atomically with the side effect, by designing operations to be naturally idempotent (setting a value rather than incrementing it), or by storing the consumer offset in the same transaction as the output. MongoDB retryable writes are a built-in example: the (lsid, txnNumber) pair lets the server recognise and skip a resent write. For transactions, an UnknownTransactionCommitResult error means you retry the commit, which is safe because commitTransaction is idempotent for the same transaction.
hint: If the ack is lost, can the sender tell whether the receiver processed the request?
explanation: The two-generals argument shows that the sender cannot tell a lost request from a lost response, so if you want no loss, retries, and therefore duplicates, are unavoidable. Exactly-once is therefore an end-to-end property: the receiver deduplicates. Interviewers want to hear "at-least-once plus idempotency", with a concrete mechanism and where the dedup state lives.

title: Sliding window log
prompt: Arrange `allow(now)` for a sliding window log: evict timestamps older than the window, reject if `limit` timestamps remain, otherwise record this request.
explanation: The log keeps one timestamp per accepted request, oldest at the front, so eviction pops from the head until everything left falls within the last `windowMs`. That gives an exact limit over any rolling window with no boundary burst: t=1299 is denied because 300, 600 and 1000 are still in the window. The cost is O(limit) memory per key, which is why large-scale limiters approximate it with a sliding window counter. In a shared store this would be a sorted set (Redis) or an array updated with `$push` and `$pull` by timestamp (MongoDB), and the evict-count-add sequence has to be atomic.

title: Sliding window counter
prompt: Fill the gaps in the sliding window counter: estimate the rolling count as the previous window weighted by its remaining overlap, plus the current window.
explanation: When a new window starts, the finished window count becomes `prevCount`; if a whole window was skipped, it is 0. At fraction `frac` into the current window, the rolling window still overlaps `1 - frac` of the previous one, so the estimate is `prevCount * (1 - frac) + curCount`, assuming traffic in the previous window was spread evenly. Like a fixed window it needs only two counters per key, but it removes most of the boundary burst: at t=1500 the estimate is 4*0.5+2 = 4, so the request is denied. Large API gateways typically use this, keeping the two counters in a shared store with atomic increments.

title: Retry on TransientTransactionError
prompt: Arrange the transaction retry loop: rerun the whole transaction only when the error carries the `TransientTransactionError` label, up to `maxAttempts`. Any other error propagates immediately.
expectedOutput:
attempt 1: WriteConflict
attempt 2: NotWritablePrimary during election
committed (commits=1)
attempt 1: DuplicateKey
gave up: DuplicateKey
explanation: MongoDB adds the `TransientTransactionError` label to errors where the whole transaction was aborted and can safely be rerun from the start (write conflicts, a primary stepping down, network errors before commit), so the application retries the entire transaction body. A DuplicateKey error has no label: retrying would fail the same way, so it propagates at once. A limit on attempts (or a deadline) stops endless retries. The driver `withTransaction` helper implements this loop plus the separate commit retry on `UnknownTransactionCommitResult`, within a 120-second overall time limit.

title: Retry storms and how to stop them
prompt: Discuss retry amplification and its mitigations.
question: A downstream service slows down and the whole system collapses into a retry storm. Explain how retries amplify load across layers, and describe the techniques (backoff, jitter, retry budgets, circuit breakers, hedged requests) that prevent it, including the trade-offs of hedging.
keyPoints: Retry amplification: retries at each of N layers multiply, e.g. 3 retries at each of 3 layers gives up to 27x load on the bottom service
Metastable failure / thundering herd: synchronised retries keep the system overloaded even after the trigger has gone
Exponential backoff with full jitter spreads retries out and desynchronises them
Retry budgets cap retries at a fraction of normal traffic (e.g. 10%) per client; retry at only one layer
Circuit breakers fail fast when the error rate is high; honour Retry-After / 429 and never retry non-transient errors
Hedged requests: send a second request after the p95 latency to cut tail latency; only for idempotent reads, and budgeted (e.g. at most 5% extra) because they add load
modelAnswer: If each layer of a call chain retries three times, a failure at the bottom of a three-layer chain can produce 3^3 = 27 times the normal load, exactly when the service is weakest. Synchronised retries then keep it overloaded after the original trigger has gone, which is a metastable failure. The first defence is exponential backoff with full jitter, so retries are spread out and clients stop retrying in lockstep. Next, cap total retries with a retry budget (for example, retries may not exceed 10% of requests over a rolling window) and retry at only one layer, normally the outermost or the one closest to the failure. Circuit breakers stop calls entirely when the error rate is high, and clients should honour 429 and Retry-After and never retry non-transient errors. Hedged requests trade the other way: after the p95 latency you send a duplicate request to another replica and take the first answer, cutting tail latency for a small amount of extra load. They are only safe for idempotent reads, such as reads from MongoDB secondaries, and they must be budgeted and must cancel the slower request, or they become a retry storm themselves. MongoDB drivers already retry reads and writes once, so application retries should take that into account.
hint: Multiply the retry counts across layers, then think about what each client does at the same moment.
explanation: The core insight is that retries are load, and they arrive exactly when capacity is lowest. Backoff with jitter fixes the timing, budgets and breakers cap the volume, and retrying at a single layer prevents multiplication. Hedging trades a limited amount of extra load for lower tail latency, which is why it must be restricted to idempotent operations and a small percentage of requests.

title: Retry budget
prompt: Fill the gaps in a retry budget that allows retries only while they stay within `ratio` of the requests seen.
expectedOutput:
requests=50 retries=5 denied=45
naive 3 retries each would add 150 extra calls
explanation: During an outage every request fails, so a naive client with three retries quadruples the traffic to the failing service. A retry budget counts original requests and allows retries only while they stay under a fixed ratio (here 10%), so at most about 1.1x normal load reaches the dependency however bad things get. When the service is healthy and failures are rare, the budget is never hit, and individual transient errors are still retried. Real implementations (gRPC, Envoy, Finagle) use a rolling window or a token bucket that deposits a fraction of a token per request, so the budget recovers over time.

title: Deadline propagation
prompt: Arrange `callService`: compute the remaining budget from the request deadline, fail fast if it is spent, cap the per-call timeout at the remaining budget, and simulate the call on a fake clock.
lines: if (remaining <= 0) throw new DeadlineExceeded(name + ": no budget left");
throw new DeadlineExceeded(name + ": timed out after " + timeout + "ms");
expectedOutput:
request with 400ms budget
  auth ok, 360ms left
  mongo-find ok, 180ms left
  pricing ok, 130ms left
request with 200ms budget
  auth ok, 160ms left
  504: mongo-find: timed out after 160ms
explanation: A deadline is an absolute point in time, set once at the edge. Every hop computes its remaining budget from it instead of using a fixed timeout, so downstream work stops as soon as the caller would give up anyway. With a 200 ms budget the find gets only 160 ms, times out, and pricing is never called, so no work is wasted on a response nobody will read. In MongoDB you pass the remaining budget down as `maxTimeMS` on the operation (or use the client-side operation timeout `timeoutMS` in newer drivers), so the server also kills the query when the budget runs out instead of running it to completion.

title: Shedding, backpressure and degradation
prompt: Discuss protecting a service under overload.
question: Your service receives 3x its capacity during a traffic spike. Explain load shedding, backpressure and graceful degradation, how they differ, and how health checks (liveness vs readiness) should behave so the load balancer and orchestrator do not make things worse.
keyPoints: Load shedding: reject excess work early and cheaply (e.g. 503/429 at admission, bounded queues, dropping by priority or queue time) to keep goodput high for the rest
Backpressure: propagate "slow down" upstream with bounded queues, blocking or credit-based flow control rather than unbounded buffering
Unbounded queues turn overload into huge latency and out-of-memory errors; shed based on queue wait time or concurrency limits, ideally adaptive (e.g. AIMD, Little's law)
Graceful degradation: serve reduced functionality, such as cached or stale data, fewer recommendations, or reads from secondaries, instead of failing completely
Liveness should only check that the process is not stuck; readiness can report overload so traffic is shifted; deep dependency checks in liveness cause restart cascades
Prioritise critical traffic and drop work whose client deadline has already passed
modelAnswer: Load shedding means deliberately rejecting the excess, cheaply and as early as possible, typically at admission with a concurrency limit or bounded queue that returns 503 or 429. It should preferably drop low-priority work or requests whose deadline has already passed. This keeps goodput near capacity instead of letting every request time out. Backpressure is the cooperative version: bounded queues and flow control push the "slow down" signal back to producers (for example, a consumer pausing reads from a stream) instead of buffering in memory until latency explodes or the process runs out of memory. Graceful degradation keeps the core path working by turning off expensive extras, serving cached or stale results, or reading from MongoDB secondaries with an acceptable read preference. Health checks need care. Liveness should only report whether the process itself is stuck: if it checks the database, a slow MongoDB makes the orchestrator restart every pod at once and remove all capacity. Readiness can fail when the instance is saturated so that the load balancer shifts traffic, but you need a guard so that all instances do not go unready at the same time. Adaptive concurrency limits, such as AIMD on latency, work better than static thresholds.
hint: What happens to latency and goodput if every request is queued instead of rejected?
explanation: Overload management is about goodput: a service that successfully serves 100% of its capacity and rejects the rest beats one that accepts everything and times out on all of it. Shedding rejects work, backpressure slows producers, and degradation does less work per request. Badly designed health checks are a classic cause of cascading failure, which senior interviewers like to probe.

title: Commit retry on unknown result
prompt: Fill the gaps so `commitWithRetry` retries `commitTransaction` only when its outcome is unknown. This is safe because commit is idempotent for the same transaction.
expectedOutput:
retry commit
retry commit
commit acknowledged
commit calls=3 applied=1
explanation: If a network error or a write concern timeout (`wtimeout`) hits during `commitTransaction`, the transaction may or may not have committed, and MongoDB labels the error `UnknownTransactionCommitResult`. You must not rerun the transaction body, which could apply it twice; you retry only the commit, which is idempotent because the server recognises the same transaction (lsid + txnNumber) and reports the original outcome. That is why the simulated server applies the change exactly once despite three commit calls. `TransientTransactionError` is the other label and means the opposite: the transaction was aborted, so the whole body is rerun. The driver `withTransaction` helper combines both loops.

title: Distributed limiter with compare-and-set
prompt: Arrange `allow` for a rate limiter shared by many app servers: read the counter document, decide, and write back with a compare-and-set on its version, re-reading on conflict so two nodes cannot both take the last slot.
lines: Doc next = new Doc(window, count + 1, cur.version() + 1);
expectedOutput:
A1: true
B1 sneaks in: true
A2: false
casFailures=1 count=2
A3 next window: true
explanation: With several app servers sharing one counter, a plain read-then-write loses updates: nodes A and B both read count=1 and both write count=2, so three requests pass a limit of two. The version check makes the write conditional, so A's write fails after B sneaks in; A re-reads, sees count=2 and correctly denies. In MongoDB you could express this as `updateOne({_id, version}, {$set: ...})` and check `modifiedCount`. Better still, put the logic in one atomic `findOneAndUpdate` with a filter like `{_id, window, count: {$lt: limit}}`, an `$inc` and an upsert for a new window, so there is no client-side loop at all. Under heavy contention on a hot key, CAS retries pile up, which is why large systems shard counters or give each node a local token allowance.

title: Tuning MongoDB driver timeouts
prompt: Design the timeout and connection pool configuration for a MongoDB-backed service.
question: An API with a 500 ms SLO talks to a MongoDB replica set. Walk through the driver settings you would tune (serverSelectionTimeoutMS, maxPoolSize, waitQueueTimeoutMS / timeoutMS, maxTimeMS, socket and connect timeouts, writeConcern wtimeout), how they interact during a primary election, and what an ambiguous wtimeout error means for the write.
keyPoints: serverSelectionTimeoutMS (default 30 s) limits how long an operation waits for a suitable server, e.g. a primary during an election (often around 10-12 s); set it within the request budget, or fail fast and degrade

maxPoolSize caps connections per server (default 100) and acts as a bulkhead; waitQueueTimeoutMS or timeoutMS limits the wait for a connection, so pool exhaustion surfaces as fast errors rather than piled-up threads

Per-operation limits: maxTimeMS makes the server abort the query; the client-side operation timeout timeoutMS in newer drivers covers the whole operation, including retries, server selection and pool wait, ideally derived from the propagated request deadline
connectTimeoutMS and socketTimeoutMS: avoid infinite socket timeouts, but do not set the socket timeout below normal query time, or healthy slow queries cause reconnect churn

wtimeout on w:majority means replication was not confirmed in time, not that the write failed; the write is not rolled back and may still commit, so treat it as unknown and reconcile or retry idempotently
Retryable writes and reads retry once after an election; with a short serverSelectionTimeoutMS the request may still succeed within its budget
modelAnswer: I would derive every timeout from the 500 ms request deadline instead of using the 30-second defaults. serverSelectionTimeoutMS controls how long an operation waits for a suitable server. During an election there is no primary for several seconds, and with the 30-second default every request thread blocks, so I lower it substantially and degrade (serve stale reads from secondaries, or fail fast) rather than queue. maxPoolSize is a bulkhead per server. I size it from the expected concurrency (Little's law: throughput times latency) and limit the wait for a connection with waitQueueTimeoutMS, or in newer drivers with the client-side operation timeout timeoutMS, which covers server selection, connection checkout, the operation and its single automatic retry, and which I set from the remaining request budget. On the server side, maxTimeMS stops expensive queries from consuming resources after the client has given up. I keep connectTimeoutMS modest and avoid a socketTimeoutMS shorter than legitimate query times, which would cause reconnect storms. Finally, a wtimeout on a w:majority write only means the acknowledgement did not arrive in time. The write was applied on the primary and may still replicate, so the outcome is unknown and must be handled idempotently (retryable writes, idempotency keys, or reading the data back), never assumed to have failed.
hint: For each setting, ask what a request thread is doing while that timer runs during an election.
explanation: Driver defaults favour eventually succeeding (30-second server selection) over meeting a latency SLO, so a production service needs settings aligned with its deadline. The connection pool is a bulkhead, server selection is where election downtime shows up, and maxTimeMS or timeoutMS carry the deadline to the server. The wtimeout ambiguity is the same "unknown outcome" problem as a lost ack, and it is solved by idempotency and retryable writes.
